headlines.summary: In John Ternus' first earnings report as CEO, Apple issued a gross margin forecast that disappointed Wall Street.
headlines.article_text: Apple earnings: John Ternus faces first test amid high memory costs Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points In John Ternus' first earnings report as CEO, Apple issued a gross margin forecast that disappointed Wall Street, sending the stock down after hours. Apple blamed higher memory prices and some costs related to Siri AI for the shrinking margins. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase," Ternus said. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Apple CEO John Ternus delivers a keynote address during the Apple Experience LA event in Los Angeles, California, on Oct. 28, 2026, introducing new Mac computer models. Frederic J. Brown | AFP | Getty Images John Ternus' first earnings report as Apple CEO was going fine until it was time to issue a forecast for the company's gross margin, one of the key metrics followed by investors. Apple reported better-than-expected earnings and revenue on Monday, including in the company's core iPhone unit, and even projected sales in the current period that topped estimates. But just before Ternus opened the earnings call up to analysts' questions, CFO Kevan Parekh came forward with the first real piece of bad news. Parekh said that for the December quarter, which goes through the holiday season, Apple's gross margin will be between 45% and 46%, trailing the 46.3% average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. "This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI," Parekh said. Apple shares slid about 2% on Tuesday. Apple stock chart It's part of an ongoing trend for Apple, which is absorbing some of the soaring costs from the global memory shortage. A margin drop in the fiscal first quarter would be a third straight decline for Apple, following a gross margin of 50.1% in the June period and 47.9% in the September quarter, boosted by 1 percentage point of tariff refunds. At the midpoint of the forecast range, it would be Apple's lowest gross margin since the fiscal fourth quarter of 2023. "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus said on the call, adding that the company is paying more than it did earlier this year. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase." Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, is grappling with a problem that his predecessor spent his final months addressing. Cook told The Wall Street Journal in June that the memory situation was a "hundred-year flood." Apple followed by raising prices across the board on Macs, iPads and accessories. In September, Apple increased the prices of its iPhones by $100, which Ternus said the company did "reluctantly." 'Less flexibility in the supply chain' Computer and smartphone makers everywhere are suffering. On Friday, Intel had its worst day on the market since the 1970s due to a weak forecast tied to the softening PC market. It's all because of insatiable artificial intelligence demand. AI server giants like Nvidia and hyperscalers are buying up all the RAM they can find, and they're willing to pay a premium for it, leaving little supply for companies that make smartphones and tablets. Despite its size and global clout, Apple said it expects supply constraints on iPhones and Macs in the holiday quarter, primarily driven by memory. On the call, Ternus had some top lieutenants field component-related questions. Sabih Khan, chief operating officer, became the first Apple COO to appear on an earnings call since Cook in 2010, when Steve Jobs was CEO. "As we have said before, we're seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal," Khan told analysts on the call. watch now VIDEO 4:06 04:06 Apple's shares remain attractive over the next 12 months, says Neuberger's Flax Squawk Box Asia In response, Apple has drastically increased its purchase obligations to secure supply, Khan said. Those obligations rose by $33 billion from the June quarter to the September period, Khan said, though he declined to answer questions about whether Apple had signed "long-term agreements" with memory makers. "We're always working hard to improve supply," Khan said. Even with the recent margin slide, Apple's gross margins are still well above where they sat earlier in the Cook era, when the number would predictably come in between 38% and 39%. As Apple's profitable services business grew, its gross margin expanded , hitting 40% in 2021 and growing from there. Analysts see a potential silver lining for Apple in the current market turmoil. Because Apple is more capable of eating a portion of the increased costs, some experts predict the company will take market share from makers of Windows PC and Android phones that don't have such a cushion. Citing data from a third-party researcher, Ternus said gains are already happening. "According to IDC, we gained share globally for the quarter and for the full fiscal year," Ternus said. "And we have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time, which is a truly remarkable testament to these incredible products." headlines.article_text: AMD (AMD) Q3 earnings report 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points AMD reported third-quarter earnings that beat Wall Street expectations, with revenue jumping 45% from a year earlier. Revenue in the chipmaker's data center business nearly doubled, and CEO Lisa Su said AMD can meet accelerating demand for AI chips. The stock is up 129% so far this year, but sold off in recent days on industrywide fears of overspending on AI infrastructure. (AMD), speaks during the company's Gamers Day event in Seoul, South Korea, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. SeongJoon Cho | Bloomberg | Getty Images Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jump 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock jumped 8% in extended trading. Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter: Earnings per share : $2.09 adjusted vs. $1.95 expected Revenue : $13.38 billion vs. $13.09 billion expected Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement . CEO Lisa Su said in a press release that she expects growth in data center processors to "accelerate further," and that meeting demand won't be a problem. "With our leadership product portfolio and deep customer and supply chain relationships, we are confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years " Su said in a statement. AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But the stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand . The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago. After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta 's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October. "Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts. PC market struggles AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI. AMD is also a major player the in weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm -based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research . AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago. For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount. AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin. Meta, Microsoft , Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering. AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung. In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications. Adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share topped the $1.03 LSEG consensus estimate, while revenue of $6.72 billion beat the $6.59 billion consensus. Freshworks earned an adjusted 22 cents per share on revenue of $245.4 million in the latest quarter, above earnings of 18 cents on revenue of $245.1 million analysts polled by FactSet were anticipating. headlines.article_text: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally on Ackman exit call Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to Bill Ackman. Both stocks have moved more than 60% higher since Oct. 14. Ackman believes both names can see a "10-fold" increase from current share prices. Bill Ackman, chief executive officer of Pershing Square Capital Management LP, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Wednesday, April 29, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman. Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign. The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday. Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship. "The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk Box ." Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Freddie Mac) over the last month. Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday. Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS. The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then. Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control. VIDEO 22:14 22:14 Watch CNBC's full interview with Bill Ackman, Pershing Square CEO President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious. The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants. Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees. Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's " The Morning Meeting " podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision. One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen. "Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said. Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling.
